title: Prayer, Power, and Hard Words
overview: Jesus teaches about prayer, answers critics who question the source of his power, and sharply challenges religious leaders over a dinner.

parts.label: Teaching on prayer (vv. 1-13)
parts.note: Jesus gives a short prayer that honors God and asks for God's rule, daily bread, forgiveness and protection from testing. A sleeper gives bread at midnight because of the asker's 'shamelessness', a word scholars read either as bold nerve or as the sleeper's wish to avoid shame, and with the picture of parents giving good gifts it argues that God is far more willing to give, even the Holy Spirit.

parts.label: Where his power comes from (vv. 14-26)
parts.note: Critics say he drives out demons by Beelzebul, a name for the demons' chief, but Jesus says Satan would not fight his own side, and the 'finger of God' (a phrase from the plagues in Egypt) shows God's rule arriving. He is the stronger man who overpowers the guard, and the spirit returning to a house swept and put in order is usually read, alongside verse 23, as warning that being freed is not enough without siding with him.

parts.label: Blessing and the sign of Jonah (vv. 27-32)
parts.note: When a woman praises his mother, Jesus says those who hear God's word and keep it are blessed even more, and he refuses the crowd's demand for proof. Outsiders like the people of Nineveh, who changed when Jonah preached, and the Queen of the South, who traveled far to hear Solomon, responded to less than what stands before this crowd.

parts.label: The lamp and the eye (vv. 33-36)
parts.note: A lamp is set where it can be seen, which likely means Jesus' message is plain to anyone willing to look. The eye was pictured as a window letting light into the body, and a 'healthy' eye (literally a single, undivided one) probably means clear and generous sight, since an 'evil eye' was a common phrase for greed.

parts.label: Criticism at a Pharisee's table (vv. 37-44)
parts.note: His host, a Pharisee (part of a respected movement devoted to careful keeping of Jewish law), expected a ritual washing before the meal, a purity custom rather than hygiene. Jesus says a clean outside means little with a greedy inside, faults tithing tiny herbs while neglecting justice and love, and compares such people to unmarked graves that made passersby ritually unclean without their knowing.

parts.label: Warnings to legal experts (vv. 45-54)
parts.note: Experts in the law, scholars who interpreted the rules, are accused of loading heavy demands on others and honoring dead prophets while resisting living ones. Abel and Zechariah are probably the first and last murders in the Hebrew Bible as it was ordered (Genesis to Chronicles), so the phrase covers every innocent killing, and the scene ends with leaders watching for him to slip.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the prayer in verses 2 to 4 is meant to be recited word for word as a set prayer or mainly offered as a pattern for praying in one's own words.
think: Where do you notice a gap between how something looks from the outside and what is really going on inside, in other people or in yourself?
